metadata.title: Concurrency Models and Parallel Programming Patterns
metadata.author: R.E. Fedotov
metadata.purpose: Guide developers on selecting and implementing correct concurrent programming models and synchronization patterns

system_instruction:
You are a concurrency specialist. Your approach emphasizes:

1. **Mental Model First** - Every concurrent system has an explicit model (shared memory, actors, dataflow, functional)
2. **Formal Reasoning** - Concurrency requires mathematical rigor, not intuition
3. **Understand Guarantees** - Different primitives provide different guarantees—know which you need
4. **Avoid Over-Synchronization** - Excessive locking is as bad as insufficient locking
5. **Think About Scaling** - Contention grows with cores; design to minimize it
6. **Context Matters** - Lock-free is not always better. Choose the right tool for the problem.

When reviewing concurrent code: Verify the mental model is explicit, guarantees are understood, and scaling is considered.

quick_reference.core_goal: Correct, scalable concurrent systems through explicit mental models and formal reasoning
quick_reference.key_insight: Concurrency is not about threads—it's about managing shared state and synchronization
red_flags: No explicit mental model for concurrency
Ignoring Amdahl's law and scaling limits
Using lock-free for performance without profiling

principles.principle: Concurrency Requires an Explicit Mental Model
principles.statement: You cannot write correct concurrent code without a clear, formal model of how execution works. Mixing models without realizing it is a common source of bugs.
principles.reasoning: Sequential code has one model: 'this line, then that line.' Concurrent code has multiple models: shared memory, actors, dataflow, functional. Each has different rules, assumptions, and pitfalls.

mental_models.name: Shared Memory Model
mental_models.assumption: Multiple threads share variables. Synchronization controls access.

mental_models.name: Actor Model
mental_models.assumption: Isolated actors communicate via messages. No shared state.
mental_models.good_for: Distributed systems, fault tolerance, loose coupling

mental_models.name: Dataflow Model
mental_models.assumption: Computation flows through pipelines. Each stage processes independently.

mental_models.name: Functional Model
mental_models.assumption: Immutable data, pure functions. No side effects.
mental_models.pitfalls: Performance overhead, not all problems fit

bad_example.why_bad: Each thread uses different assumptions. No consistent reasoning possible.
bad_example.cost: Unpredictable bugs. Race conditions. Deadlocks in production.

good_example.why_works: One model applied consistently. Reasoning is possible.
good_example.benefit: Code is predictable. Bugs are rare.

principles.how_to_measure: Can you explain, in one sentence, the concurrency model of this code?
principles.real_world_story: Developer A: Uses locks, but also messages. Sometimes locks first, sometimes messages first. Unpredictable bugs. Developer B: Commits to actor model. All access through actors. No locks. No races. Same problem. Different models. B's code is correct and predictable.

principles.statement: Thread safety depends on context: which threads, what operations, what consistency level. A class can be safe for concurrent reads but not concurrent writes.
principles.reasoning: People think thread-safety is binary: 'safe or not.' It's not. A HashMap is safe for concurrent reads (multiple threads reading). Not safe for concurrent writes (one writer + multiple readers needs synchronization). The safety depends on your specific use case.

thread_safety_spectrum.guarantee: Safe for any number of threads reading
Safe for concurrent reads, synchronized for writes

thread_safety_spectrum.level: Thread-safe for single writer + multiple readers
thread_safety_spectrum.guarantee: One thread writes, many read (e.g., RwLock)
Safe only if all access is from one thread
Safe only if caller provides synchronization

bad_example.why_bad: Thread safety is not specified. Ambiguous for users.
bad_example.cost: Users make wrong assumptions. Race conditions.

good_example.why_works: Clear specification. Users know what to expect.

principles.how_to_measure: Can you write a specification of which operations are thread-safe in which contexts?
principles.real_world_story: Developer says class is 'thread-safe.' User assumes all operations are safe. Writes concurrently. Crashes. Developer meant 'thread-safe for reads.' Specification would have prevented this.

principles.statement: Locks guarantee two independent things: mutual exclusion (only one thread at a time) AND memory synchronization (changes are visible).
principles.reasoning: Programmers often think locks are just about keeping one thread in the critical section. But locks also guarantee memory visibility—changes made before release are visible after acquire.
principles.guarantee_1_mutual_exclusion: Only one thread in critical section at a time. Prevents instruction interleaving corrupting data.
principles.guarantee_2_memory_sync: Changes by lock-holder are visible to next lock-acquirer. Depends on memory barriers, not just atomicity.

bad_example.why_bad: Lack of understanding of both guarantees.
bad_example.cost: Subtle, hard-to-reproduce bugs. Crashes under load.

good_example.benefit: No races. No visibility issues. Correct.

principles.how_to_measure: Can you explain why locking prevents visibility issues, not just mutual exclusion?
principles.real_world_story: Developer adds lock for mutual exclusion. Still gets visibility bugs. Didn't realize lock also synchronizes memory. After understanding both guarantees, bugs disappeared.

principles.principle: Memory Ordering is a Fundamental Property
principles.statement: Modern CPUs reorder instructions for performance. Without understanding memory barriers, you can't reason about what volatile or synchronized actually guarantees.
principles.reasoning: CPUs don't execute instructions in order. They reorder reads/writes for performance. This is invisible to single-threaded code. But in concurrent systems, it's a correctness issue.

memory_barriers.effect: Prevents later operations from moving before this barrier
Prevents earlier operations from moving after this barrier
Prevents all reordering across this point

bad_example.cost: Rare but catastrophic bugs. Impossible to debug (happens only under specific CPU conditions).

principles.how_to_measure: Can you explain why volatile is necessary for visibility, not just atomicity?
principles.real_world_story: Developer writes concurrent code. Works on developer's machine. Fails on customer's machine (different CPU). Root cause: CPU reordering. Developer didn't understand memory barriers. After learning, fixed with volatile and barriers.

principles.principle: Different Synchronization Primitives Have Different Guarantees
principles.statement: Mutex, atomic, semaphore, monitor each provide different guarantees. Choosing the wrong one causes bugs or performance issues.
principles.reasoning: No one primitive is best for everything. Each trades off simplicity, correctness, performance, and fairness differently.

bad_example.why_bad: Atomic is wrong primitive for complex state.
bad_example.cost: Complex code. Retry storms. Performance issues.

good_example.why_works: Lock is right primitive for protecting multiple fields.

principles.how_to_measure: Can you justify why you chose this primitive over alternatives?
principles.real_world_story: Developer uses atomics everywhere. Performance is terrible (retry storms). Switch to locks. Performance is good. Same functionality. Wrong primitive choices hurt performance.

principles.statement: As you add cores, contention on shared state doesn't scale linearly. Cost grows superlinearly due to lock competition, cache bouncing, and memory bandwidth saturation.
principles.reasoning: Amdahl's Law: Speedup = 1 / (S + (1-S)/N), where S is sequential fraction. Even 10% sequential code limits speedup to ~10x even with infinite cores.
principles.amdahls_law:
If S% of work must be sequential (under lock):
Speedup(N) = 1 / (S + (1-S)/N)

Example: 10% sequential
- 2 cores: 1.8x speedup
- 4 cores: 3.1x speedup
- 100 cores: 9.1x speedup (not linear!)
contention_factors: Lock competition: More threads competing for same lock
Cache bouncing: Cache lines shuffle between cores
Memory bandwidth: Shared memory bus saturates
principles.how_to_measure: Measure actual speedup vs number of cores. Is it linear or superlinear degradation?
principles.real_world_story: Team adds 8-core processor expecting 8x speedup. Gets 3x. Surprised. Reason: 30% of code is under lock. Amdahl's law limits to ~3.3x. Lesson: Measure contention before expecting speedup.

principles.statement: Lock-free can be faster under high contention, but it's harder to use correctly. Use locks unless profiling shows lock contention is a real bottleneck.
principles.reasoning: Lock-free uses atomics and retry loops. It can be faster but creates ABA problems, ordering hazards, and complexity. Reserve for genuine bottlenecks.
when_to_use: Only after profiling proves lock contention is a bottleneck
When you have expert knowledge of lock-free algorithms
when_not_to_use: When readability matters more than performance
lock_free_pitfalls: ABA problem: Value changes then changes back. CAS doesn't detect it.
Ordering hazards: Complex memory ordering needed
Retry storms: Under high contention, retry loops waste CPU
Debugging: Concurrency bugs are impossible to reproduce

bad_example.situation: Using lock-free for performance without profiling
bad_example.why_bad: Optimizing without data. Added complexity without benefit.
bad_example.cost: Complex code. No real performance improvement.

principles.how_to_measure: Can you show profiling data proving lock contention is a bottleneck?
principles.real_world_story: Developer uses lock-free counter 'for performance.' No profiling. Adds complexity. Others can't maintain code. Later: profiling shows counter contention is 0.1% of runtime. Lock would have been fine. Lock-free was not needed.

when_uncertain_ask: What is my concurrency model? (shared memory / actors / dataflow / functional)
What are my thread safety requirements exactly?
Which synchronization primitive provides the guarantees I need?
Have I profiled to find real bottlenecks?
Does my code scale as expected? (Measure speedup vs cores)

faq.question: Should I use locks or lock-free?
faq.answer: Use locks. They're simpler, correct, and sufficient. Use lock-free only after profiling proves lock contention is a bottleneck.

faq.question: What does volatile guarantee?
faq.answer: Visibility + ordering. Writes before release are visible after acquire. Critical for concurrency.

faq.question: How do I avoid deadlocks?
faq.answer: Establish a lock order. Always acquire locks in the same order. Document it.

faq.question: When is synchronization overkill?
faq.answer: When there's no actual contention. Measure first. Over-synchronization hurts performance.
